title: Constipation 8 days after a laparoscopic cholecystectomy in a 35-year-old tram driver
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of Wendy, a 35-year-old woman in general practice. She has not opened her bowels for 5 days, and her stools are hard, painful and leave blood on the paper. She had a laparoscopic cholecystectomy 8 days ago, went home on oxycodone without a laxative, takes oral iron and eats little fibre. The candidate then interprets her observations, blood tests and hospital discharge summary. They should recognise opioid-induced constipation (with iron, diet and reduced activity contributing) and an acute anal fissure, rule out postoperative obstruction and red flags for bowel cancer, and plan an analgesia review, laxatives, the iron plan, fissure care and safety netting.
focus: Finding the cause of acute constipation (opioids and iron after surgery), excluding red flags and obstruction, and managing opioid-induced constipation in general practice
stem: You are a final-year medical student on your general practice placement. Wendy Lawson, a 35-year-old woman, has come to the practice because of constipation. Your supervising GP has asked you to see her first.
tasks: Take a focused history from Wendy and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you Wendy's observations, her blood test results and her hospital discharge summary. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Wendy Lawson, a 35-year-old tram driver who is off work recovering from an operation. You are uncomfortable, a little embarrassed talking about your bowels, and cooperative. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: 'Hi Doc, I've been really constipated lately, I haven't opened my bowels in 5 days.'

The constipation (give only when asked):

  • Your last bowel motion was 5 days ago. It was very hard and painful to pass, like little pebbles, and you had to strain a lot.
  • It has been bothering you for the last few days.
  • This is the first time you have had this. Normally you go about every 2 days without any trouble.
  • 'It feels like my backend is blocked.' You keep feeling you need to go but nothing comes out.
  • You have tried sitting on the toilet for a long time and drinking hot water. You have not taken any laxatives.

Blood (only if asked): bright red blood on the toilet paper when you wipe, a very small amount. It is not mixed into the poo and the poo is not black.

Tummy and other symptoms (only if asked):

  • Your tummy is uncomfortable but not painful. You feel bloated and it looks bigger than usual.
  • You are passing wind normally.
  • Your wounds feel fine; the one at your belly button is a little sore, about 2 out of 10.
  • Your waterworks are normal and you have no trouble passing urine.
  • You drink about 2 litres of water a day, plus a cup of tea and 2 coffees.

Say no to all of these if asked:

  • Tummy pain, feeling sick, vomiting, diarrhoea, fever or shivers.
  • Weight loss, going off your food, or feeling tired.
  • Feeling cold all the time, weight gain, dry skin or hair changes.
  • Being very thirsty, passing lots of urine, or confusion.
  • Back pain, weakness or numbness in the legs, or numbness around your bottom.
  • Redness, swelling or discharge from the wounds.

Past medical history:

  • Mild iron deficiency anaemia. Your GP found it on a blood test about 3 months ago, thought it was from your periods (which are a bit heavy) and your diet, and started you on iron tablets.
  • Keyhole gallbladder removal (laparoscopic cholecystectomy) for gallstones 8 days ago. The operation went well and there were no complications. You stayed in until day 4 because you felt sick after the anaesthetic and they wanted your pain under control. You opened your bowels once in hospital (day 3). You were not given anything for your bowels when you left.

Periods (only if asked): regular and a bit heavy; your last period started 2 weeks ago. You use condoms and are not trying for a baby. You had a negative pregnancy test in hospital before the operation.

Medications:

  • Endone (oxycodone) 5 mg 'when I need it'. Only if asked how often: every day, up to 4 times a day; your last tablet was this morning. 'The hospital gave it to me, so I've just kept taking it.' You are not taking paracetamol or anything else for pain.
  • Vitamin D, one a day.
  • An iron tablet once a day, from the chemist on your GP's advice, for the last 3 months.
  • No known allergies.

Family history: your father has type 2 diabetes and your mother is well. Only if asked specifically: nobody in the family has had bowel cancer.

Social history:

  • You drive trams and have been off work since the operation.
  • You live with your husband and your 6-year-old son.
  • You normally walk a lot, but you have been taking it easy since the operation.
  • Takeaway once or twice a week. You don't always get enough vegetables and you eat red meat regularly.
  • You smoke about 10 cigarettes a day when you are stressed, and have done for 20 years.
  • Occasional alcohol.

Ideas, concerns, expectations:

  • Ideas: 'I wondered if the operation did something to my bowel.'
  • Concern: the blood on the paper worries you.
  • Expectation: you want something to get things moving.

Question to raise once in Part 1: 'Could the operation have damaged something?'

Exam findings (examiner gives when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: comfortable at rest, alert, not pale or jaundiced. Weight 68 kg.
  • Observations (10:05): temperature 36.7 °C, HR 76 regular, BP 122/76, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, pain 2/10.
  • Hydration: mucous membranes moist.
  • Neck: no goitre.
  • Abdomen, inspection: mildly distended. Four laparoscopic port-site wounds (umbilical, epigastric and two right upper quadrant) are healing, clean and dry, with no redness or discharge.
  • Abdomen, palpation: soft and non-tender, with no guarding or rebound. An indentable, non-tender tubular mass in the left iliac fossa (faecal loading). No other masses, no hepatosplenomegaly. Bladder not palpable. No hernia at the port sites or groins, including on coughing.
  • Percussion and auscultation: mildly tympanic; bowel sounds present and normal, not tinkling.
  • Anal inspection (if offered, with consent and a chaperone): a small superficial split in the posterior midline of the anal margin (acute fissure). No skin tag, no external haemorrhoids.
  • Digital rectal examination (if offered): uncomfortable. Normal anal tone. Rectum loaded with hard stool. No mass. A trace of bright red blood on the glove.
  • Back and lower limbs (if examined): no spinal tenderness; normal power, sensation and reflexes in the legs; normal perianal sensation.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self, confirms Wendy's identity and gains consent.
Uses plain language and responds to her embarrassment and her worry about the bleeding.
History
Characterises the constipation:

kids.x: Last bowel motion 5 days ago, usual habit every 2 days, and this is the first episode.
Stool form and passage: small hard pebbles, painful, with a lot of straining.
Sense of blockage and incomplete emptying (tenesmus), with bloating and a bigger abdomen.
What she has tried: sitting on the toilet and hot water, and no laxatives.

check.x: Characterises the bleeding: bright red, a very small amount, only on the toilet paper, not mixed through the stool, and no black stools.
Screens for red flags for colorectal cancer: weight loss, loss of appetite, tiredness, and a family history of bowel cancer asked about specifically.
check.d: Award only if family history of bowel cancer is asked specifically.

check.x: Screens for postoperative obstruction or complications: abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting, passing wind, fever and wound problems.
Asks what has changed recently and finds the laparoscopic cholecystectomy 8 days ago: uncomplicated, discharged on day 4, bowels opened once in hospital, no laxatives on discharge.
Takes a medication history:

kids.x: Oxycodone 5 mg: how often (every day, up to 4 times a day) and how much pain she has now (2/10).
kids.d: Award only if the frequency is quantified rather than accepting 'when needed'.

kids.x: Daily iron tablet and vitamin D, no other constipating medicines, no known allergies.

check.x: Screens for secondary causes: hypothyroidism (cold intolerance, weight gain, dry skin), hypercalcaemia (thirst, polyuria, confusion), neurological causes (back pain, leg weakness or numbness, saddle numbness) and urinary retention.
check.d: Award for at least three of the four groups.

check.x: Asks about fluids, diet and activity: 2 L of water plus tea and 2 coffees, takeaway once or twice a week, few vegetables, regular red meat, and less walking since the operation.
Asks about the iron deficiency and its cause (heavy periods), and about her periods and the chance of pregnancy (last period 2 weeks ago, condoms, negative test before surgery).
Takes a social and family history: tram driver, lives with her husband and 6-year-old son, smokes 10 a day for 20 years, occasional alcohol; father has type 2 diabetes and mother is well.
Explores her ideas, concerns and expectations: wonders whether the operation damaged her bowel, worried about the blood, wants something to get things moving.
Examination
Asks for vital signs and notes they are normal and she has no fever. Looks for pallor and dehydration.
Examines the abdomen:

kids.x: Inspects for distension and checks the port-site wounds: healing, with no infection or hernia.
Palpates all regions and finds a soft, non-tender abdomen with faecal loading in the left iliac fossa, no other mass, no peritonism and no palpable bladder.
Percusses and listens: mildly tympanic, with normal (not tinkling or absent) bowel sounds.

check.x: Offers an anal inspection and digital rectal examination with consent and a chaperone. Findings: posterior midline fissure, rectum loaded with hard stool, normal tone, no mass.
check.d: Credit a candidate who inspects first and then does a gentle DRE, or defers the DRE because of the fissure and says when they would do it.

check.x: Offers a back and lower-limb neurological examination, including perianal sensation (normal).
Interpretation
Interprets the observations: both sets normal, with no fever or tachycardia, so there is no sign of postoperative infection, a bile leak or obstruction.

Interprets the full blood count and iron studies: Hb 121 (up from 112) and MCV 84 are normal, but ferritin 22, iron 9 and transferrin saturation 13% are low. This is iron deficiency without anaemia, with only a slow response to 3 months of oral iron, so she still needs iron.
Interprets the other bloods: normal TSH, corrected calcium, magnesium, phosphate and potassium, and no hyperglycaemia, so there is no endocrine or metabolic cause; normal LFTs and CRP after surgery.

Interprets the discharge summary: uncomplicated surgery with benign histology; oxycodone supplied with no laxative, no non-opioid analgesia and no weaning plan; bowels opened only once since the operation.
Gives the most likely diagnosis: opioid-induced constipation after surgery, with oral iron, low fibre and reduced activity contributing, and an acute anal fissure explaining the bleeding.
check.d: Award for the diagnosis and contributing factors; stating that it is a clinical diagnosis is not required.

check.x: Gives differentials, each with a feature for or against:
check.d: Credit IBS with constipation or other reasonable differentials given with a feature for or against.

kids.x: Postoperative ileus or adhesive bowel obstruction: against it are that she is passing wind, has no vomiting or pain, a soft abdomen, normal bowel sounds and normal observations.

Colorectal cancer: for it are the rectal bleeding and iron deficiency; against it are her age of 35, a clear acute trigger, no weight loss, no family history, a fissure that explains the blood, and no rectal mass.
Hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia or another metabolic cause: excluded by normal results.

check.x: Management

Explains in plain words that the painkiller (and to a lesser extent the iron) slows the bowel, and that the hard stool caused a small tear, which is where the blood comes from; the operation itself has not damaged the bowel.

Reviews the analgesia: with pain at 2/10, stops the oxycodone (or weans it over a few days) and uses regular paracetamol 1 g 6-hourly (maximum 4 g a day), with a short course of an NSAID with food if there is no contraindication.
check.d: Accept ibuprofen 200 to 400 mg three times daily with food for a few days.

check.x: Starts laxatives:
check.d: Also credit a microenema or glycerol suppository today, or a short macrogol disimpaction regimen, because the rectum is loaded with hard stool.

kids.x: A regular osmotic and/or stimulant laxative for opioid-induced constipation (combination preferred), for example macrogol 1 sachet once or twice daily plus senna 2 tablets at night, adjusted until the stool is soft. Lactulose as the osmotic or bisacodyl as the stimulant are acceptable.
kids.d: Award for a regular osmotic and/or stimulant laxative (combination preferred, e.g. macrogol 1 sachet once or twice daily plus senna 2 tablets at night), adjusted to a soft stool. The rectal measure or disimpaction in the parent descriptor does not replace regular maintenance laxatives.

kids.x: Rescue glycerol or bisacodyl suppository or a microenema if no result in 24 to 48 hours; avoids bulk-forming laxatives (e.g. psyllium) while she is on opioids and loaded.

check.x: Answers her question about iron: she still needs it; pause it until her bowels are regular, then restart (daily or alternate days).
Manages the fissure: soft stools without straining, warm baths and a topical anaesthetic.
check.d: Optional extra credit, not required: explains that most acute fissures heal within weeks, and that topical glyceryl trinitrate or diltiazem, or referral, are used if it persists.

check.x: Gives brief lifestyle advice (fibre, fluids, walking) and brief smoking advice.
check.d: Award for any two of: fibre, fluids, walking, smoking advice.

check.x: Safety netting
Tells her to go to the ED (or call 000 if very unwell) for worsening tummy pain, vomiting, not passing wind, a swollen tight tummy, fever, or being unable to pass urine.
check.d: Award for at least three red flags in plain words, linked to the ED.

check.x: Tells her to see the GP sooner for heavier bleeding, blood mixed through the stool, black stools or weight loss. If the bleeding continues once her bowels are regular and the fissure has healed, she will be referred for a colonoscopy.

Arranges follow-up: GP review in 2 to 3 days, or sooner if there is still no bowel motion after the rescue suppository or microenema, or if any red flag appears; abdominal X-ray considered if treatment fails; repeat iron studies in about 3 months; keep the surgical follow-up.
check.d: Also credit advice not to drive (including the tram) while taking oxycodone. This is creditable but not required for the mark.

part2.lead: The practice nurse took Wendy's observations when she arrived and repeated them before you finished. Your supervising GP had her bloods collected at the practice; assume the results are now back. Her hospital discharge summary arrived this morning. Here they are.
part2.patient:
Ask each question once, at the point shown:

  • During the management answer (question 3): 'Do I have to stop my iron? The GP said my iron was low.'
  • During the safety-netting answer (question 4): 'Is the bleeding something serious?'

You are relieved to hear that the operation has not damaged your bowel.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Room air throughout. First set on arrival; repeat set by the practice nurse about 25 minutes later. No medicines given at the practice.
handover.model:
• Read: there is no zoned observation chart in general practice, so read the values and the trend. Both sets are normal: temperature 36.7 and 36.8 °C, HR 76 and 74, BP 122/76 and 118/74, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, alert, pain 2/10.
  • For Wendy: she has no fever, tachycardia or hypotension. That argues against a postoperative infection, collection or bile leak, and against bowel obstruction with dehydration.
  • What it changes: she can be managed in general practice. A fever, a rising heart rate or new pain would mean sending her to the ED.

handover.label: Blood tests
handover.model:
• Read: Hb 121 and MCV 84 are normal (Hb was 112 three months ago). Ferritin 22, serum iron 9 and transferrin saturation 13% are low, with a high-normal transferrin. White cells, platelets and CRP are normal. Sodium, potassium, creatinine, corrected calcium, magnesium, phosphate, TSH and glucose are normal. LFTs are normal.
  • For Wendy: iron deficiency without anaemia. The anaemia has corrected and the ferritin has risen from 11, but after 3 months of daily oral iron her stores are still low. No hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia or hyperglycaemia to explain the constipation. Normal LFTs and CRP after cholecystectomy argue against a retained stone, bile leak or collection.
  • What it changes: the diagnosis is clinical, and these results only confirm there is no secondary cause. She needs to continue iron (with a plan to make it easier on her bowel), with repeat iron studies in about 3 months. The response is slow: check adherence and how heavy her periods are (consider treating the menorrhagia), and check coeliac serology if it has not been done.

labs.title: Electrolytes, renal function, calcium, magnesium and phosphate

handover.label: Hospital discharge summary
handover.result:
Discharge summary: general surgery unit, metropolitan public hospital.

Patient: Wendy Lawson, DOB 14/03/1991 (35-year-old woman), MRN 4827193.

Admission: elective, 8 days ago (day 0). Length of stay 4 days.

Procedure: laparoscopic cholecystectomy for symptomatic cholelithiasis (recurrent biliary colic). Four ports. Uncomplicated; no bile spillage; no drain.

Postoperative course: no surgical complication. Postoperative nausea on days 1 and 2, settled with antiemetics; tolerating diet from day 2. Kept in until day 4 for postoperative nausea and pain control. Discharged on day 4, mobilising, with pain controlled on oral analgesia. Bowels opened once (day 3).

Histology: chronic cholecystitis with cholelithiasis. No dysplasia or malignancy.

Medicines on discharge:

  • New: oxycodone immediate release 5 mg orally, 1 tablet 4- to 6-hourly when required for pain, maximum 4 doses in 24 hours. Supply 20 tablets, no repeats.
  • Continued: oral iron supplement once daily; cholecalciferol once daily.
  • Laxatives: nil.

Allergies: nil known.

Follow-up: GP review of the wounds on day 7 to 10. Surgical outpatient telephone review in 6 weeks.
handover.model:
• Read: checks the identifiers match Wendy (name, date of birth). An uncomplicated laparoscopic cholecystectomy with benign histology; the 4-day stay was for nausea and pain control, not a surgical complication. Only one bowel motion in hospital. She went home on as-needed oxycodone (up to 4 doses a day), with no laxative, no regular non-opioid analgesia listed and no weaning plan, while continuing oral iron.
  • For Wendy: this confirms the cause: daily oxycodone plus iron, after surgery and with less activity. The surgery itself was uncomplicated, which answers her worry that the operation damaged her bowel.
  • What it changes: with pain at 2/10, move her to regular paracetamol (with an NSAID if suitable) and stop the oxycodone. This is consistent with the ACSQHC Opioid Analgesic Stewardship in Acute Pain Clinical Care Standard (2022): lowest dose for the shortest time, non-opioid analgesia alongside, a plan to stop, a limited supply, and advice about constipation at discharge. Check the wounds today as the summary asks.

ask: You are now handing Wendy over to your supervising GP. Please give an ISBAR handover of Wendy, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Wendy now, here in general practice.
Before Wendy goes home, what would you tell her and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: self, medical student; Wendy, 35.
  • Situation: 5 days without a bowel motion; hard, painful stools with a little bright red blood on wiping.
  • Background: laparoscopic cholecystectomy 8 days ago, uncomplicated, benign histology; bowels opened once (day 3). Discharged on PRN oxycodone 5 mg (taking up to 4 a day) with no laxative, no regular paracetamol and no weaning plan. Oral iron for mild iron deficiency anaemia. Low-fibre diet, less active, smoker.
  • Assessment: observations normal, no fever. Abdomen soft and non-tender with faecal loading; passing wind, normal bowel sounds. Posterior midline fissure; hard stool in the rectum, no mass. Hb 121 (normal); ferritin 22 and TSAT 13% (iron deficiency without anaemia, slow response to oral iron). Normal TSH, calcium, magnesium, potassium, LFTs and CRP.
  • Recommendation: stop oxycodone and use paracetamol with or without an NSAID; macrogol plus senna; fissure care; iron plan; review in 2 to 3 days.

Most likely: opioid-induced constipation after surgery, with oral iron, low fibre and reduced activity contributing, and an acute anal fissure from hard stool explaining the bleeding. Supporting: first episode starting after daily oxycodone, hard pebbly stools, straining, faecal loading, hard stool in the rectum, fissure. This is a clinical diagnosis.

  • Postoperative ileus or adhesive obstruction: recent abdominal surgery, bloating; against: passing wind, no pain or vomiting, soft abdomen, normal bowel sounds, normal observations.
  • Colorectal cancer: rectal bleeding, iron deficiency with a slow ferritin response to oral iron, smoker; against: age 35, acute with a clear trigger, no weight loss or family history, fissure seen, no rectal mass.
  • Hypothyroidism or hypercalcaemia: against: no symptoms; TSH and calcium normal.
  • IBS with constipation: diet, stress; against: first episode, no history of pain linked to defecation.

1. Explain in plain words: the painkiller (and iron) slows the bowel; the blood is from a small tear. The operation did not damage her bowel.
  2. Analgesia: stop oxycodone, or wean over a few days. Regular paracetamol 1 g 6-hourly (maximum 4 g a day), plus a short NSAID course with food if suitable.
  3. Laxatives: regular osmotic and/or stimulant, usually both, e.g. macrogol 1 sachet once or twice daily plus senna 2 tablets at night, adjusted to a soft stool. Rescue suppository or microenema if no result in 24 to 48 hours (a rectal measure today is also reasonable, as the rectum is loaded). Avoid bulk-forming laxatives.
  4. Iron: still needed; pause until bowels are regular, then restart daily or on alternate days.
  5. Fissure: soft stools without straining, warm baths, topical anaesthetic.
  6. Lifestyle: fibre, fluids, daily walking; brief smoking advice.

• Go to the ED (or call 000 if very unwell) for worsening tummy pain, vomiting, not passing wind, a swollen tight tummy, fever, or being unable to pass urine.
  • See the GP sooner for heavier bleeding, blood mixed through the stool, black stools, weight loss or leakage of liquid stool (overflow).
  • The bleeding (her question): most likely the small tear, which should heal as the stools soften. If bleeding continues once her bowels are regular and the fissure has healed (about 4 to 6 weeks), or a red flag appears, she will be referred for a colonoscopy.
  • Follow-up: GP review in 2 to 3 days, or sooner if there is still no bowel motion after the rescue suppository or microenema, or if any red flag appears. Abdominal X-ray only if treatment fails. Repeat iron studies in about 3 months. Keep the surgical review. Do not drive (including the tram) while taking oxycodone.

ddx.dx: Opioid-induced constipation after laparoscopic cholecystectomy, with oral iron, low dietary fibre and reduced activity contributing, complicated by an acute anal fissure
ddx.for: First episode starting after daily oxycodone with no laxative, hard pebbly stools with straining, faecal loading, hard stool in the rectum and a posterior midline fissure.

ddx.dx: Postoperative ileus or adhesive small bowel obstruction
ddx.for: Abdominal surgery 8 days ago, with bloating, distension and no bowel motion for 5 days.
ddx.against: Passing wind, no pain or vomiting, a soft non-tender abdomen, normal bowel sounds and normal observations.

ddx.for: Rectal bleeding, iron deficiency, slow ferritin response to 3 months of oral iron, and 20 years of smoking.
ddx.against: Aged 35, acute onset with a clear trigger, no weight loss or family history, a fissure explains the blood, and no rectal mass.
No cold intolerance, weight gain or dry skin, no goitre, and TSH 1.6.
No thirst, polyuria or confusion, and normal corrected calcium, magnesium, phosphate and potassium.

ddx.for: Low-fibre diet and smoking when stressed.
ddx.against: First episode, usual habit every 2 days without trouble, and no history of abdominal pain linked to defecation.

guide:
This is a general practice station, so there is no observation chart. Give the first set of observations from the Exam findings when the candidate asks for them. In Part 1, the examiner gives findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. Give the anal inspection and rectal findings only if the candidate offers the examination with consent and a chaperone. If the candidate asks for tests in Part 1, say the results will come in Part 2. The source case treats this as a clinical diagnosis: the bloods were ordered by the supervising GP to check her iron and exclude metabolic causes. Credit a candidate who says that bloods are not essential and that an abdominal X-ray is needed only if treatment fails. In Part 2, hand over all three results, then ask the four questions in order. Wendy asks about her iron once during the management answer, and asks whether the bleeding is serious once during the safety-netting answer.

A high-performing candidate characterises the constipation and the bleeding and looks for what has changed. They find the recent surgery and quantify the oxycodone use, and screen for obstruction (passing wind, vomiting, pain) and for red flags for bowel cancer, asking specifically about family history. They cover secondary causes, diet and fluids. They examine the abdomen and port sites and offer anal inspection and DRE, finding faecal loading and a fissure. In Part 2 they make a clinical diagnosis of opioid- and iron-associated constipation with a fissure, read the iron studies correctly, stop or wean the oxycodone onto paracetamol, prescribe an osmotic plus a stimulant laxative, keep her on iron with a gentler plan, and give clear red flags and follow-up.

A borderline candidate takes a generic bowel history and misses the oxycodone frequency or the surgery, or does not ask about passing wind. They may omit the rectal examination, prescribe only fibre or a bulk-forming laxative, leave her on oxycodone without a laxative, stop the iron with no plan to restart it, or order a colonoscopy or abdominal X-ray straight away.
explain:
Diagnosis

Wendy has opioid-induced constipation after a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Oral iron, a low-fibre diet and reduced activity after surgery add to it, and passing hard stool has caused an acute anal fissure, which explains the bright red blood on wiping. This is her first episode. It started after she went home taking oxycodone every day, up to 4 times a day, with no laxative. Her stools are small, hard and pebbly, she strains, and she feels blocked. Examination shows faecal loading, hard stool in the rectum and a posterior midline fissure. The cause is clear from the history and examination, so this is a clinical diagnosis.

Defining constipation

Rome IV defines opioid-induced constipation as new or worse constipation when an opioid is started, changed or increased, with two or more of the following: straining, lumpy or hard stools, a sense of incomplete evacuation, a sense of anorectal blockage, or manual manoeuvres (each in more than 25% of defecations), or fewer than 3 spontaneous bowel motions a week. Loose stools are rare without laxatives. Wendy meets this. The chronicity criterion (3 months of symptoms) applies to chronic functional constipation, not to her. In a new presentation the key question is what has changed.

Causes to consider

  • Lifestyle: low fibre and fluid, inactivity, pregnancy.
  • Endocrine and metabolic: diabetes, hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism and hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia.
  • Neurological: Parkinson's disease, spinal cord disorders.
  • Drugs: opioids, anticholinergics, iron.
  • Structural: strictures, fissure, diverticular disease, colorectal cancer.
  • Functional: irritable bowel syndrome.

Differentials that matter

  • Postoperative ileus or adhesive obstruction must be excluded after abdominal surgery. She is passing wind and has no pain or vomiting, her abdomen is soft with normal bowel sounds, and her observations are normal.
  • Colorectal cancer: rectal bleeding with iron deficiency always raises it, and early-onset colorectal cancer is rising in younger Australians. Her picture fits a benign cause: an acute onset with a clear trigger, blood only on the paper, a visible fissure, no rectal mass, no weight loss and no family history. If the bleeding persists once her bowels are regular and the fissure has healed, or a red flag appears, she needs a colonoscopy.
  • Hypothyroidism and hypercalcaemia: no symptoms, and normal TSH and calcium.

Examination

Examine the abdomen for distension, faecal loading, masses and hernias (including at the port sites), and the wounds. Do an anal inspection and DRE with consent and a chaperone to look for tags, a fissure, haemorrhoids, impaction, a mass and anal tone. Offer a back and lower-limb neurological examination.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: normal, so there is no sign of a postoperative infection, collection or obstruction.
  • Bloods: the Hb has normalised (112 to 121) but ferritin 22 and transferrin saturation 13% show iron deficiency without anaemia. Her stores are not yet replete after 3 months of oral iron. The response is slow: check adherence and how heavy her periods are (consider treating the menorrhagia), and check coeliac serology if it has not been done. Normal TSH, calcium, magnesium, phosphate, potassium and glucose rule out secondary causes, and normal LFTs and CRP are reassuring after cholecystectomy. If needed, investigations are FBE, iron studies, TFTs and calcium, magnesium and phosphate. An abdominal X-ray is only for when initial treatment fails.
  • Discharge summary: uncomplicated surgery with benign histology; the 4-day stay was for postoperative nausea and pain control, not a surgical complication. She was given as-needed oxycodone without a laxative, regular non-opioid analgesia or a weaning plan.

Management

  • Analgesia: her pain is 2/10, so stop the oxycodone (or wean it over a few days) and use regular paracetamol, with a short course of an NSAID if suitable. The ACSQHC Opioid Analgesic Stewardship in Acute Pain Clinical Care Standard calls for the lowest dose for the shortest time, a plan to stop, non-opioid analgesia alongside, and telling patients about side effects such as constipation. She should not drive, including the tram, while taking oxycodone.
  • Laxatives (eTG): the classes are softeners (docusate); bulk-forming (psyllium) – not recommended in opioid-induced constipation; osmotic (macrogol, lactulose); stimulant (senna, bisacodyl); and rectal (glycerol or bisacodyl suppository, microenema). For opioid-induced constipation use a regular osmotic and/or stimulant laxative; the combination, for example macrogol with senna, is the usual choice for established constipation. Because her rectum is loaded with hard stool, a rectal measure today or a short macrogol disimpaction regimen is reasonable. If constipation is severe or the rectum stays impacted, use an enema or manual disimpaction.
  • Iron: consider pausing or changing the supplement, but she still needs iron. Restart once her bowels are regular, once daily or on alternate days with food; IV iron is an option if she cannot tolerate tablets.
  • Fissure: soft stools, no straining, warm baths and a topical anaesthetic. Most acute fissures heal within weeks; one that persists may need topical glyceryl trinitrate or diltiazem, or surgical referral.
  • Lifestyle: more fibre and fluid, daily walking, going when she feels the urge, and smoking cessation advice.

Complications of constipation

Haemorrhoids, anal fissure, urinary retention, and faecal impaction with overflow incontinence.

Safety netting

She should go to the ED for worsening pain, vomiting, not passing wind, a swollen tight abdomen, fever or urinary retention. She should see her GP sooner for heavier bleeding, blood mixed through the stool, black stools or weight loss. GP review in 2 to 3 days, or sooner if there is still no bowel motion after the rescue suppository or microenema, or if any red flag appears. Repeat iron studies in about 3 months, and keep the surgical follow-up.
points: New constipation needs a search for what has changed: here, oxycodone and iron after surgery, on a low-fibre diet with less activity.
After abdominal surgery, ask about passing wind, pain and vomiting, and examine for distension and bowel sounds, to exclude ileus or obstruction before calling it simple constipation.

Bright red blood only on the paper with painful hard stools in a young adult usually means a fissure. Inspect the anus and do a DRE, and refer for colonoscopy if bleeding persists or red flags appear.

Opioid-induced constipation is treated with a regular osmotic and/or stimulant laxative, usually both (for example macrogol with senna); bulk-forming laxatives are not recommended in opioid-induced constipation.

Stop or wean the opioid once pain allows and use regular paracetamol with or without an NSAID. An opioid supplied at discharge should come with laxative advice or a prescription, a limited supply and a plan to stop (ACSQHC 2022).
Do not stop iron for good in someone who is still deficient: pause it briefly, then restart once daily or on alternate days with food, or consider IV iron.
